transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it’s... it’s a bit of a hard thing for me to admit, to be honest with you. I’ve always been a guy who handles his business, you know? I drive a truck for a living, out on the road a lot, making deliveries, and out there you have to be reliable. You have to be steady. People count on you to keep the rig on the road and get the job done. 

But there's this thing I do with food. I just... I eat a whole lot all at once. And what really brings me in today, what finally made me pick up the phone and make this appointment, is what happens right after I do it. When it's over, I’ll just sit there—maybe in the cab of my truck at a rest stop, or alone at my kitchen table after a long shift—and I’m just looking at all the empty containers. The wrappers, the takeout boxes, the bags just piled up there in front of me. 

And this wave of... I just feel so completely disgusted with myself. I mean, deeply, deeply ashamed. I sit there staring at the trash and I feel like I'm not the steady, in-control man I've always tried to be. I've spent my whole life, all fifty-nine years, trying to be the guy who keeps his hands on the wheel, literally and figuratively, you know? And then I look at those empty containers and I just hate myself for it. I feel like I have absolutely zero willpower. It’s just this heavy, sickening feeling of disgust that sits in my chest, and it's getting to be too much to carry around anymore.
After these episodes of eating a lot, do you ever make yourself vomit, take laxatives, or exercise excessively to try to control your weight or how you feel about yourself?

No, no, I don't do anything like that. I've heard of people doing that, you know, making themselves sick or running for miles and miles, but that's not me. I don't throw up. I've never bought a laxative in my life, wouldn't even know which aisle they're in at the pharmacy. And as for exercise, well, my job keeps me sitting behind the wheel of a rig for ten, twelve hours a day, so I'm not exactly hitting the gym after a long haul. 

I just... I just sit there with it. The food, I mean. It just sits in my stomach, like a rock, and I just have to deal with how uncomfortable I am, physically and mentally. I'll be in the sleeper berth of my truck, and my stomach will be stretched so tight it hurts, and I just lie there feeling miserable. I don't try to undo it or burn it off. I just take the punishment, I guess. I just let the guilt and the physical pain wash over me until it finally passes, which sometimes takes hours. But no, I don't try to purge it or anything like that. I just live with the aftermath.
When you eat a lot all at once, do you feel like you can't stop yourself or control how much you're eating during that time?

Yeah. Yeah, that's exactly it. That's... that's the part that really scares me, to be honest with you. Because out there on the highway, I’m in charge, right? I’ve got seventy or eighty thousand pounds of freight behind me, and I have to be completely dialed in. I have to anticipate every brake light, every lane change, every gust of wind coming across the plains. Total control. 

But with this... it's like a switch flips in my brain. Once I start, it feels like the exact same discipline I have on the road just completely shuts off. It’s just gone. It's like I'm not even in the driver's seat of my own body anymore. I'll be sitting there, maybe in a corner booth at a truck stop diner or just huddled in the back of my cab, and I'm literally having an argument with myself in my own head. I'm sitting there, and even while I’m telling myself, "Magin, put the fork down. You don't need this, you're already full, just stop," my hand keeps going back for more. 

It's like it has a mind of its own. I’ll be chewing and swallowing and reaching for the next bite all at the exact same time, knowing I should stop, wanting to stop, but I just... I can't. It’s like a runaway truck on a steep downgrade and the brakes are completely shot. I just have to ride it out until it crashes, until every last crumb of the food is gone. I'll be staring at my own hand, watching it bring another handful of chips or another slice of pizza to my mouth, and I just don't understand how a man my age can't even tell his own arm to stop moving. It's terrifying, doc. It really is.

When you're having one of these episodes or thinking about them, does your weight or body shape play a big role in how you feel about yourself, or do you feel particularly upset about those aspects of your appearance?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I think a lot of people assume that's what it is. That I'm sitting there obsessing over my waistline or worrying about how I look in the mirror. But to be completely honest with you, doc... no. It's not really about my weight or my shape at all. I mean, sure, I'm a big guy, and sitting in a truck all day doesn't exactly do wonders for your physique, but I've never been the type to stand in front of the mirror and pinch my belly or worry about fitting into a certain size pair of jeans. I'm fifty-nine years old, I wear comfortable clothes for work, and I've sort of just accepted the body I have. 

When I get so upset after I eat like that, it's not because I'm thinking, "Oh no, I'm going to gain five pounds," or "I'm going to look fat." It's not about the outside. It's entirely about the inside. It's about the fact that I let myself lose control. Like I was saying before, about being the guy who keeps his hands on the wheel... that's what eats at me. It's the weakness. It's the feeling that I'm a grown man who can't even govern his own actions for twenty minutes. 

I'll be sitting there in the cab, looking at the wrappers, and I'm not thinking about my belt size. I'm thinking about how pathetic it is that I couldn't stop myself. I'm thinking about how I let this... this urge just completely hijack me. It's a failure of discipline, a failure of character, really. That's where the disgust comes from. It's a deep, deep disappointment in myself as a man, not as someone trying to win a beauty contest. So, no, my weight or my shape... they really don't cross my mind when I'm in the middle of it, or even afterward when I'm beating myself up about it. It's all about the loss of control.
How often do these episodes happen, and have they been happening regularly over a longer period of time?

Well, doc, to give you the full picture, you gotta understand that my whole routine has been completely shot lately. I’m actually off the road right now. I’ve been stuck at home because of a back injury—blew it out about three months ago, and you know how that goes at my age. You spend half your life sitting in a truck seat vibrating down the interstate, your spine takes a beating, and then one wrong twist and you’re laid up. So, I’ve been cooped up in the house, mostly just confined to my recliner, trying not to aggravate it. And since I’ve been home with this injury... man, the eating, it's just gotten so much worse. 

When you’re not working, the days just kind of bleed into each other, you know? The house is quiet, there's no logbook, no dispatch calling, and that’s when it gets me. I’d say it’s been happening several nights most weeks. I'll be sitting there watching TV, trying to ignore my back, and then that switch flips. Monday night, maybe Wednesday, then Friday... it just keeps happening. 

I've been trying to wrap my head around it, trying to remember if I've had any good stretches, but honestly? Looking back over these past three months since I got hurt, I can’t think of a single week where I didn’t have at least one of those episodes. Not one. And usually, like I said, it’s a lot more than just one. It’s like without the structure of the job keeping me in line, I just completely fall apart. I’ll tell myself on Sunday, 'Alright, this week is going to be different, you're going to hold it together,' and then by Tuesday night I'm sitting in the dark surrounded by empty boxes and wrappers again. Three solid months of this, week in, week out. You'd think the back pain would be the worst part of being off work, but no... it's this. It's just exhausting.
Have you ever felt significant distress about your weight or body shape during these episodes, or has your main concern been about losing control while eating?

Well, like I was trying to explain just a bit ago, doc, no. It really never is about the weight or the shape of my body. I know it probably sounds a little crazy, because you look at a guy eating a whole family-sized pizza and a couple boxes of snack cakes in one sitting and you just assume he must be sitting there hating his gut, but... I really don't care about the gut. I mean, I'm fifty-nine years old. My back is completely blown out. I'm not exactly trying to impress anybody down at the beach, you know? 

The distress... the real, gut-wrenching distress that I feel during all of this... it is one hundred percent about the control. Just the control. It's that awful feeling of being completely hijacked. I'll be sitting in that same brown recliner, the one I'm practically chained to right now because of my back, and I'm just watching my own hands do the work. My mind is screaming at me to stop, telling me I'm full, telling me it's ridiculous, but my hands just keep moving from the wrapper to my mouth. That's the part that makes me feel sick to my stomach, not the calories or the scale. 

I've spent my entire adult life being the guy people rely on to get the freight from point A to point B safely, on time, with absolutely no excuses. If it's a white-out blizzard up in the Rockies, I get out, I put the chains on the tires, and I handle it. I control the machine. I always control the machine. But with this food thing... the machine is controlling me. And that right there, that total loss of the steering wheel in my own life, that's what keeps me up at night hating myself. So no, it's never the weight. It's just... it's just the sheer weakness of it all. I just can't stand being weak.
